evidence.claim: A prairie drive linking two wetlands on the Central Flyway
evidence.quote: The Wetlands and Wildlife National Scenic Byway crosses the Central Flyway

evidence.claim: linking two wetlands
evidence.quote: This 77-mile central Kansas Byway connects two of the world's most significant natural wetlands — Cheyenne Bottoms and Quivira National Wildlife Refuge.

evidence.claim: The Wetlands and Wildlife National Scenic Byway curves past Cheyenne Bottoms and Quivira National Wildlife Refuge, crossing the Central Flyway in central Kansas.
evidence.quote: It curves around Cheyenne Bottoms and Quivira Refuge.

evidence.claim: Kansas Tourism lays out a 77-mile drive from Hoisington to St. John, using K-4, K-156 and local roads.
evidence.quote: Distance: 77 miles Hoisington to St. John (North to South)

evidence.claim: The byway organization identifies the wetlands as stopovers for millions of migrating birds each year, including waterfowl, shorebirds and whooping cranes.
evidence.quote: More than 60,000 acres of wetlands host millions of migrating birds each year, including waterfowl, shorebirds, even Whooping Cranes.

evidence.claim: At Cheyenne Bottoms, the struggle to direct water preceded the scenic route.
evidence.quote: In 1900, a project known as the Koen Ditch attempted to divert Arkansas River water 12 miles (19 km) to the Bottoms so that it could be used for irrigation.

evidence.claim: The Koen Ditch project attempted to bring Arkansas River water to the basin for irrigation in 1900, but a flood washed the ditch out.
evidence.quote: In 1900, a project known as the Koen Ditch attempted to divert Arkansas River water 12 miles (19 km) to the Bottoms so that it could be used for irrigation. The ditch washed out in a flood.

evidence.claim: Plans in the 1920s reversed the idea: drain the Bottoms for farmland. Downstream residents in Hutchinson protested that this would create flooding problems.
evidence.quote: During the 1920s, various plans were put forth to drain the Bottoms and convert it to farmland. However, residents downstream in Hutchinson, Kansas protested that doing so would create flooding problems for them.

evidence.claim: Begin in Hoisington and head east on K-4 toward Cheyenne Bottoms.
evidence.quote: Begin your journey in Hoisington at the intersection of US-281 and K-4. Head east on K-4 towards the Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Refuge.

evidence.claim: The route then turns south on NE 100 Avenue to K-156 before continuing along local roads toward Quivira.
evidence.quote: Make a right and head south on NE 100 Ave. Stay on NE 100 Ave for about 4 miles until you reach the intersection of K-156 and NE 100 Ave.

evidence.claim: Beyond the refuge, it follows Raymond Road south and NE 70th Street west, finishing at US-281 just north of St. John.
evidence.quote: The route concludes just north of St. John where NE 70th St intersects with US-281.

evidence.claim: using K-4, K-156 and local roads
evidence.quote: Turn right on K-156 and remain on the road for about 4 miles until you are at the K-156 and NE 30 Rd intersection.

evidence.claim: continuing along local roads toward Quivira.
evidence.quote: Make a left on NE 140th St towards the Quivira National Wildlife Refuge.

evidence.claim: it follows Raymond Road south and NE 70th Street west
evidence.quote: Keep heading south on Raymond Rd. for 7 miles until you reach the intersection for NE 70th St and Raymond Rd. At this intersection, turn right onto NE 70th St. Remain on NE 70th St, heading west for 16 miles.

evidence.claim: The basin is natural; the divisions across it are engineered. Cheyenne Bottoms occupies a land sink, with its wetland pools separated by dikes.
evidence.quote: The entire wetland occupies a natural land sink spanning 41,000 acres or 64 square miles (170 km2). Of that area, 19,857 acres (80.36 km2) constitutes the Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Area. The Bottoms is impounded and divided into a set of pools by a network of dikes.

evidence.claim: Historically, it has alternated between lake, mudflat and dry ground.
evidence.quote: Historically, Cheyenne Bottoms has been a lake of varying size, a mudflat, or dry.

evidence.claim: A new canal from the Arkansas River arrived in 1957, but drought and competing water claims limited how much reached the wetland.
evidence.quote: In 1957, a new canal from the Arkansas River was built.  However, relatively little water from the Arkansas was pumped into the wetland because of drought and claims by other entities on the water supply.

evidence.claim: Renovations in the 1990s subdivided the marshes to make them more self-sustaining, though water supply and water-level management remain critical problems.
evidence.quote: In the 1990s, an extensive renovation subdivided the marshes. The renovations allowed the marshes to be more self-sustaining, although an adequate water supply and management of water levels continue to be critical problems.

evidence.claim: Migrating shorebirds feed on the mudflats.
evidence.quote: Cheyenne Bottoms is especially noted for the concentration of migratory shorebirds that come here to feed on the mudflats.

evidence.claim: Dikes divide the wetland into pools, with mudflats, ponds and islands beside them.
evidence.quote: Surrounding the pools are mudflats, ponds, and islands.

evidence.claim: Salt marshes distinguish Quivira, where Rattlesnake Creek supplies the main flow of water.
evidence.quote: The Refuge is bisected by Rattlesnake Creek from which it receives the main flow of water.

evidence.claim: Big Salt Marsh and Little Salt Marsh are shallow lakes, and 21 miles of constructed canals create additional marshland.
evidence.quote: It has two shallow lakes, Big Salt Marsh and Little Salt Marsh, that have attracted migratory birds and animals for centuries. Twenty-one miles (34 km) of canals have been constructed to create additional marshland.

evidence.claim: The refuge was created in 1955.
evidence.quote: Quivira National Wildlife Refuge was created in 1955

evidence.claim: Its name comes from a fabled city of gold sought by Francisco Vásquez de Coronado in 1541.
evidence.quote: The name Quivira derives from a fabled Native American city of gold.  In 1541 Spanish conquistador Francisco Vásquez de Coronado led an expedition onto the Great Plains of Kansas searching for wealth.

evidence.claim: He spent a month with the Quivirans, ancestors of the Wichita tribe, before returning to New Mexico without gold.
evidence.quote: He spent a month with the Quivirans, the ancestors of the Wichita tribe, but returned to New Mexico without finding any gold.

evidence.claim: The refuge’s sand prairie combines plants from eastern tallgrass and western shortgrass prairie.
evidence.quote: The sand prairie has species from both the eastern Tallgrass prairie and the western Shortgrass prairie or steppe.

evidence.claim: Salt marshes distinguish Quivira
evidence.quote: Its proximity to the Central Flyway migration route and the salt marshes on the refuge combine to endow the refuge with a large variety of birds.

evidence.claim: St. John began with a different name and a religious purpose. In 1875, William Bickerton of the Church of Jesus Christ founded a colony here called Zion Valley.
evidence.quote: The first settlement in what is today St. John was made in 1875 when William Bickerton of the Church of Jesus Christ founded a religious colony named Zion Valley.

evidence.claim: By 1879 it had grown into a small town, and residents renamed it for Governor John P. St. John to gain favor in the contest for Stafford County’s seat.
evidence.quote: By 1879, Zion Valley had grown into a small town, and the residents renamed it St. John, after then governor John P. St. John, in order to gain favor in winning the county seat of Stafford County.

evidence.claim: St. John remains the seat of Stafford County.
evidence.quote: St. John is a city in and the county seat of Stafford County, Kansas, United States.

evidence.claim: The spelling became another civic project: residents secured a correction in 2015 after the Postal Service had changed the official listing to “Saint John” in the 1970s.
evidence.quote: In 2015, due to diligent work of local citizens and former local graduates, the official government listing of locations has been corrected to spell the town correctly as "St. John" instead of "Saint John" that was incorrectly changed by the United States Postal Service in the 1970s.

evidence.claim: Kansas created its Forestry, Fish and Game Commission in 1925 to develop and care for the Bottoms.
evidence.quote: In 1925, the Kansas Forestry, Fish and Game Commission was created to develop and care for the Bottoms.

evidence.claim: Federal wildlife-restoration legislation in 1937 then made development funds available through taxes on sporting arms and ammunition.
evidence.quote: Following the Pittman–Robertson Federal Aid in Wildlife Restoration Act of 1937, which taxed sporting arms and ammunition, funds became available to develop the Bottoms.

evidence.claim: Blood Creek and Deception Creek feed the basin from the northwest; a canal brings another inflow from Walnut Creek.
evidence.quote: Its primary inflows are two small local streams, Blood Creek and Deception Creek, which flow into it from the northwest. Its other inflow is an inlet canal from Walnut Creek to the southwest.

evidence.claim: Winter wheat and milo are also grown on refuge land, with part of the crop left for wildlife.
evidence.quote: Another 1,200 acres (4.9 km2) of Refuge land is farmed with winter wheat and milo. A portion of the crop is left in the fields for wildlife.

evidence.claim: Dikes divide the wetland into pools
evidence.quote: The Bottoms is impounded and divided into a set of pools by a network of dikes.

evidence.claim: crossing the Central Flyway
evidence.quote: The Wetlands and Wildlife National Scenic Byway crosses the Central Flyway

evidence.claim: in central Kansas.
evidence.quote: This 77-mile central Kansas Byway

flags: No cached page supplies the road’s builders, designation campaign or construction chronology; the historical paragraph therefore covers documented water-management history along the corridor.

Dropped the current implication that Blood Creek was named for an 1825 battle. The cache labels the battle a legend, gives conflicting Kiowa/Pawnee identification, and does not explicitly establish the naming. No community source is cached.
Kansas Tourism gives 77 miles; FHWA gives 76.7, consistent with rounding. Tourism’s opposing directions give different K-156 leg lengths; omitted that precision and the old practical note.

Quivira road lengths and observation tower occur only in Wikipedia; omitted present visitor arrangements because no refuge-manager page is cached. Wichita tribe naming follows that source; no tribal account is available.
